content_en:
Following last week’s release of Carbon and Hydrogen, Google today is rolling out Gemini 4 Neon. The model offers “frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.”

Before today, Google’s Gemini 4 family consisted of:

- **Hydrogen** — Everyday help: Flash replacement
- **Argon** — Code & analysis: “…ideal choice for the *majority* of software engineering and knowledge work”
- **Carbon** — Most complex work: “…built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence”

Neon has performance comparable to, if not surpassing, Carbon across coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks, but at Flash speeds and a lower cost.

As such, Neon is available in the Gemini app for AI Pro (and AI Ultra) subscribers, with 3.1 Pro finally going away. Neon also replaces Argon. Meanwhile, 3.5 Flash-Lite is now “Auto” in the model picker for paid users.

With this launch, the model picker is:

- **Auto**: Adapts to your needs
- **Everyday help**: 4 Hydrogen
- **Deeper analysis**: 4 Neon
- **Code & complex work**: 4 Carbon

In the Gemini app, Google says to expect:

- **Higher-quality writing and knowledge work:** Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs.
- **Reliable research and analysis:** Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data.
- **Faster help for tougher tasks:** Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund.

Neon has the same 1 million-token context window with four thinking levels, like Hydrogen: Low, Medium, High, and Extra High. Officially, the new model sits between Hydrogen and Carbon in the Gemini 4 family.

Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency.


In terms of benchmarks:

- Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models.
- Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index.
- …reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench.
- Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI, ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following.
- It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts…
- …performs on par with leading models on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%).
- It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs’ Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business.
- …it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena’s new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.
- Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).
- …ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6)
- score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1
- 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0.

Neon is priced at $3/1M input tokens and $15/1M output tokens, or twice as expensive as Hydrogen. Argon and Carbon cost $2/1M input and $10/1M output until November 30. After the promotional pricing, it will be $4/1M input and $20/1M output, with Neon 25% cheaper as a result.

The model is also available in Google Antigravity for paid AI Pro or Ultra subscribers.

title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Neon, with "fast end-to-end task completion" across coding, knowledge work, and science, in the API, Antigravity, and the Gemini app

content_en:
# Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index, Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index. Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.

Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app.

## Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work

Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index, it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench.

Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI, ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).

## Built for production-ready code

Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.

Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0. For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.

## Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows

We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.

Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.

## Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense

As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).

Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2, Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.

To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models.

- **Finding code vulnerabilities:** Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge.
- **Validating risk through exploitation:** To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon.
- **Patching vulnerabilities:** Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2, driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon.

Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program.

## Designed for safe, dependable execution

Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack— maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on:

- **Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks:** Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science.
- **Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior:** In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation.
On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels.

content_en:
### Google upgrades Gemini’s agentic Task mode with new model, e-commerce features

Google LLC is releasing a new version of its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant that is better at performing multistep tasks.

Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Tuesday blog post.

The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs. The first, Chat, generates quick, relatively simple responses to prompts. The second mode, which is called Task, enables Gemini to perform complex tasks such as booking appointments and comparing online product listings. Task is the focus of this week’s update.

Google is switching the feature to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its newest large language model. It’s somewhat less capable than Gemini 4 Carbon, the search giant’s most advanced LLM, but significantly more cost-efficient. Hydrogen is also fast: Google says it can process some tasks 2.8 times faster than its previous entry-level model.

One way Hydrogen reduces wait times is by parallelizing project steps that are usually performed one after another. According to Woodward, users of Gemini’s Task mode can give the model feedback after each step to guide its work. The model proactively asks users for instructions before performing a sensitive task such as making an online purchase.

Today, Gemini’s Task mode uses Google Wallet to process transactions. Woodward said that the search giant is working with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to add support for a technology called payment tokenization. It replaces the user’s card number with a placeholder value called a token. That token is shared with merchants instead of the card number to reduce the risk of data leaks.

Google also plans to add support for a second technology called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It makes it easier for AI agents such as Gemini to interact with online stores and thereby lowers the risk of errors.

Gemini’s Task mode can use data in other Google services such as Gmail to inform its decisions. For example, the agent might take the user’s past purchases into account when generating shopping suggestions. One of Gemini’s main selling points is that it can use such data without moving it off Google infrastructure, which is often not the case with competing agents.

“When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users,” Woodward wrote. “Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams.”

Google has made Gemini’s Task mode free in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India as part of the update. That’s notable because Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC charge for the comparable features they offer as part of their chatbot services. Google’s move may prompt them to revise their pricing.

title_en: Anthropic Prices IPO Shares At $83, Above Range
excerpt_en: The offering promises to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals.
content_en:
Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday afternoon, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing, CNBC, Reuters and the Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.

The offering promises to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is slated to begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares, bringing in about $66.4 billion.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, the IPO and private placement total more than $92 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX, by comparison, raised $75 billion in its June offering.

## **Fast growth but no profits, yet**

The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books.

For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago.

Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

title: Anthropic reportedly prices IPO at $83 a share, above projected range

title_en: Anthropic reportedly prices IPO at $83 a share, above projected range
excerpt_en: The long-awaited IPO reportedly values the company at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis.
content_en:
Anthropic has reportedly priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round, but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.

Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.

The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce plans for an IPO.

Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the company, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers. Investors that own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Spark Ventures, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company.

Some of the company’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they were reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO.

Yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the Claude maker’s strategic partners, Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.

The company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each.

### Google Cloud brings AI agents to the supercomputing bottleneck

High-performance computing, or HPC, is merging with artificial intelligence faster than many research teams can adapt. Compute capacity is hard to get, and workloads now run across clouds and on-premises clusters. The metric that matters is shifting from peak performance to time to discovery.

That shift is on full display as supercomputing and AI converge at SC26 in Chicago. Researchers need more compute than any single site can provide, and cloud providers are now pitching AI agents as the layer that ties scattered resources together, according to Annie Ma-Weaver (pictured, left), head of high-performance computing product at Google Cloud, a unit of Google LLC.

“We are powering that flexibility. and we understand that researchers really need access to compute, but they don’t necessarily wanna learn all the nitty-gritty of how to tie that compute together, how to get it orchestrated across all their different clusters,” Ma-Weaver said.

Ma-Weaver and Megan Gawlik (right), high-performance computing product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents are simplifying access to distributed computing resources, changing simulation and weather forecasting and raising questions about researchers’ reliance on AI-generated results. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### **Agentic HPC shifts the focus from flops to discovery**

Google Cloud builds its agentic HPC strategy on three pillars: purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration such as Slurm and Kubernetes, and collaborative AI agents, Ma-Weaver explained. The company laid out the approach in its SC26 announcements. Agents now help scientists comb through research literature, debug code and generate hypotheses in minutes instead of weeks, according to Gawlik.

“You’re able to go explore more scenarios and you might be using that same time to just go sanity test that hypothesis that’s coming out,” Gawlik said. “I think it’s not only a speed thing, but I think it’s an accuracy thing that you’re able to really get from that additional speed.”

Simulation is changing as well. Engineers used to run simulations across an entire parameter space. Now they can use AI up front to decide which candidates are worth testing, Ma-Weaver noted.

“What we’re seeing, for example, with computer-aided engineering, is that you can actually identify ahead of time which are non-essential parameters and you don’t run the simulation, thereby reducing the total simulation time,” she said. “We also find that if you’re doing design and you have initial prototypes, you can generate new, novel and creative prototypes.”

The gains are already reaching weather forecasting in production. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s forecasting platform has heavy, tightly coupled workloads and once ran only on-premises, but it now runs on Google Cloud, Ma-Weaver explained. The National Hurricane Center also used Google’s WeatherNext model to predict the path and intensity of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, Gawlik noted. But the growing reliance on AI-generated results also carries a risk for younger researchers, who may lean on machine output instead of developing critical-thinking skills, she added.

“AI is still not perfect,” Gawlik said. “I think even though there’s an output, we call it AI slop. It could still be slop.”

content_en:
New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to *The New York Times*. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the *Times* that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

# The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search

Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the *Times*, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to *The Verge*, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

excerpt_en: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella expressed confidence in Jensen Huang's successor Colette Kress, who is serving as Nvidia's interim CEO.
content_en:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies.

“It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report.

While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft.

“I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette \[Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia\] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before \[Huang left\], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”

Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO.

“Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill \[Gates\]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.”

# OpenAI opens its AI systems to four independent on-site auditors for the first time

**OpenAI is giving four outside audit organizations direct access to its internal AI systems to investigate safety risks and model behavior on-site.** The company says it's working with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire, as OpenAI announced. The program builds on an earlier on-site review of its monitoring systems and fulfills commitments from the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."

Depending on their assignment, the organizations get access at OpenAI's offices to unreleased models, source code, training data, and monitoring systems. They can also speak confidentially with developers. Apollo Research is examining whether models secretly work against their developers' intentions. METR is reviewing AI misbehavior in the largest reinforcement learning training run, a method where models learn through rewards. Goodfire is analyzing internal model processes, and Transluce is evaluating post-training safety checks. OpenAI and Transluce are also planning an eight-week follow-up review for early 2027.

An independent safety board oversees the entire process, receives unredacted reports, and mediates disputes. The auditors publish their findings independently, but OpenAI can redact confidential material and delay reports to fix risks first. The company expects some friction early on but is already considering more reviews, including ones focused on company culture and internal processes.

content_en:
**Perry AI**, the London-based startup building an AI-powered legal operating system for private equity and venture capital funds, has raised €2 million ($2.2 million) in a Seed funding round.

The round was led by Haatch, with participation from Antler, Syncorp Ventures, Araya Ventures, US super angel Kelsey Chase, and a cohort of strategic angel investors. The company says the Seed funding round was oversubscribed, driven by strong interest in the LegalTech space, with funding surpassing €2.09 billion ($2.3 billion) in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

“*The biggest wins in AI will go to companies that go deep in markets where the stakes are high and generalist tools fall short. Private capital legal work is a textbook example. Shashwat and Vaneesa have spent nearly three decades between them doing this work, and it shows in the product: Perry AI doesn’t just review documents, it builds a living memory of every commitment a fund has made and acts on it. The early customer results are exceptional, and we’re delighted to lead this round as Perry takes its platform to the next level*,” said **Fred Soneya**, co-founder and General Partner at Haatch.

Perry AI was founded in 2025 by Shashwat Patel and Vaneesa Agarwal, who together bring nearly three decades of private capital legal experience. Patel spent 15 years as a funds and corporate lawyer at Debevoise & Plimpton and Simmons & Simmons, advising major asset managers including BlackRock, Brookfield, and Invesco. Agarwal, an NYU School of Law graduate, built a venture capital law firm from scratch to 75 deals and a top-tier Legal 500 ranking within three years.

With Perry AI, they are building and maintaining a live legal memory for private capital markets, one capable of capturing every right, obligation, side letter commitment, and negotiated position a fund has made, across every deal. AI agents then act on that record, reviewing documents, flagging issues, preparing drafts, and coordinating in-house teams with external counsel through one shared, live workspace.

The platform covers the full fund lifecycle, from fund formation and capital deployment to portfolio and fund management, and exit. It serves both fund teams and the law firms advising them. Perry AI says law firms can also white-label the platform under their own brand, keeping clients engaged for the life of a fund rather than only during live transactions.

“*I spent more than 15 years advising funds, and every deal had the same undercurrent: a scramble against the clock, in a high-stakes, regulated world, with the constant fear that something had been missed. A side letter promise, a consent or preemption right, an MFN obligation buried three deals back. Generic AI can’t take that fear away, because it doesn’t know the fund. Perry AI does*,” said **Patel**, co-founder and CEO of Perry AI.

He added, “*It remembers every position a fund has taken and acts on it, so legal teams can move fast and still sleep at night. Demand has been exceptional, and this round lets us build on our momentum in Europe and take Perry AI across the US and Asia*.”

The company says funds already using Perry AI manage over €1.4 billion ($1.5 billion) in assets under management across more than 1,000 portfolio companies. Its users report working 90% faster, with deal signing times on live transactions reduced from 84 days to just 13 days,

The fresh capital will accelerate Perry AI’s expansion into the United States and Asia, while deepening its European and UK growth. The company also plans to extend the platform beyond deal execution into areas such as fund formation, secondaries, fund transfers, LP reporting, MFN tracking, and co-invest allocation, several of which are already live.

title: PwC’s IPO Lead On A Selective Market, AI Valuations And The Outlook For 2027
excerpt: In this Q&A, Mike Bellin, a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. title_en: PwC’s IPO Lead On A Selective Market, AI Valuations And The Outlook For 2027
excerpt_en: In this Q&A, Mike Bellin, a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027.
content_en:
The U.S. IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven. Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings.

Mike Bellin, a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation.

In a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027.

*This interview has been edited for length and clarity.*

**Crunchbase News: How healthy is the IPO market right now?**

**Bellin:** A good IPO year in the U.S. is anywhere from 125 to 175 traditional IPOs, and year to date we’ve seen just south of 90 or so.

The breadth of the market shows me that it’s been a healthy market. We’ve seen industrial products come back to market. We’ve seen tech, consumer markets, energy, utilities and some financial services come back to market.

For the majority of the first three quarters of the year, it was a pretty strong and broad IPO market. But the momentum has halted significantly since September and October.

Is the market in trouble? I would say no. It’s very selective. It’s not shut. Quality issuers with readiness, the right story, the right metrics can still get their deals done.

**What has contributed to the slowdown?**

**Bellin:** The macro environment in general was the big mover: rates, inflation, geopolitical concerns. Just that uncertainty was a big factor.

One of the big factors that I’ve seen is valuation. Some fairly aggressive valuations were being asked for in certain transactions, certain offerings, and I think the market — with all those uncertainties that I mentioned — was looking at those valuations and thinking it was maybe a bit rich.

I believe many issuers decided to hit pause and wait for another window to open.

**What are public market investors looking for?**

**Bellin:** What investors are really looking for is durable revenue — revenue that’s backed up by strong customers, diverse customers and a growing revenue base. I think it’s that revenue reliability where there is a significant backlog of demand for the product, the services of the IPO issuer. That’s always a strong sign.

The other item is leverage. For companies with significant leverage in a rising-rate environment, the questions are: Can they take on new leverage that creates profitable value opportunities going forward? Can they refinance existing leverage given rates are higher?

Making sure that you’re going into the capital markets with a reasonable leverage ratio, or explaining through your equity story how you’re getting a return on the capital that you have invested from a debt perspective, makes a significant difference.

**Is the market open to a broad range of venture-backed startups, or primarily larger companies?**

**Bellin:** Scale matters. Companies that have that scale, whether it’s from a revenue perspective or an asset-based perspective, depending on the sector, make a big difference. Those are the types of companies that can almost dictate the window that they’re going to go out in and do well.

Some of the smaller companies, the midmarket companies, smaller-cap companies — again, outside of life science and biotechs — they’ve been a little bit challenged.

If you’re growing at the right rate, you’re showing the right metrics, the IPO market is fully available to those types of companies. But if you’re still on the lower-scale side of the house, your opportunities may be limited to hit the market.

**Will enthusiasm for AI companies carry into public markets, or will investors be more skeptical?**

**Bellin:** I think investors aren’t skeptical of AI; they’re skeptical of spend without visibility — visibility to future earnings, visibility to that revenue durability that I mentioned.

The market is separating AI companies with visible demand from the ones with only a narrative out there, and I think that demand, that growth, the backlog is key.

The other factor we’re seeing in today’s market again comes down to cash generation and profitability. If you’re not profitable, when will that profitable period come? Profitability comes in many different measures. Could be GAAP income, could be EBITDA income, but also cash flows and free cash flows and levered free cash flows that are available to the company.

We haven’t seen a period like this of development, of growth, ever before. It’s exciting, but I do think the market will discern between those companies that are public-company worthy and those that are not.

**What does the uneven performance of newly public companies signal?**

**Bellin:** It signals selectivity. There have been some really big winners in the IPO market, and others that, post-issuance, haven’t traded as well as many expected.

Many of the companies that are coming to market have to be very thoughtful on the valuation and what you’re going to go price at. If you’re trying to be too aggressive on pricing, you may trade down post-IPO, which is going to impact those metrics.

Overall, we’re seeing strong candidates come to market. I do think companies are coming to market better prepared now than ever, given this volatility.

**What is driving biotech’s resurgence?**

**Bellin:** The M&A market for many of these companies is very strong today. As some of the larger health company names lose the patents to some of the profitable drugs, they’re looking at that next generation of development and where there could be value.

Many of these biotechs were purchased by large pharma companies even before coming to the public markets. That competition for these assets and companies is creating a nice horse trade between an IPO opportunity with a lot of upside and an M&A exit with more certainty day one.

I think M&A is the engine behind the IPO market’s resurgence for these companies.

In the IPO markets, many of these assets have traded very well, and that’s where the momentum and that flywheel effect in the IPO market is very important. We’ve seen that flywheel and that momentum in biotech. We haven’t seen it in the rest of the market in the last couple of months.

**Why are SPACs attracting renewed interest?**

**Bellin:** With market volatility, we’re seeing more conversations around SPACs. Because SPACs set valuation certainty on day one, a company looking to exit via SPAC understands the potential cash that may come their way. It’s not certain, of course, given redemptions, etc.

Another factor driving a healthy SPAC market may be these serial SPAC issuers. They understand the SPAC product. They understand what makes a good de-SPAC candidate, and they know whether the target company can be ready, show growth and hit the milestones that may be discussed in the offering document.

The market is healthier and more mature today than in the past. That said, we’re still seeing many SPACs continue to look for a target, given the massive SPAC inventory available to target companies.

**What do you expect in 2027?**

**Bellin:** Hundreds of companies are in the pipeline, and they’re ready to go when the market is. Much of the remainder of ’26, and the start of 2027, depends on market momentum.

I’m an eternal optimist. There’s a lot of demand on the buy side; there’s still significant capital available to the right companies. So if we can create that momentum here in the remaining months of 2026, I think we’re going to see a strong start to 2027.

title: Palo Alto inks $4.5 billion deal for AI startup Applied Compute, shares pop 7% on earnings

content_en:
Palo Alto Networks shares jumped more than 7% after the cybersecurity firm beat Wall Street's fiscal first-quarter estimates and inked a deal for artificial intelligence startup Applied Compute.

Here's how the company did versus LSEG estimates:

- **Earnings per share**: $1.05 adjusted vs. 97 cents expected
- **Revenue**: $3.44 billion vs $3.31 billion expected

Revenue jumped 39% from $2.47 billion in the year-ago quarter.

Fears of AI-powered cyberattacks, heightened by incidents like the Hugging Face breach, are driving demand for cybersecurity vendors like Palo Alto Networks. Amid this backdrop, the company's shares have jumped 85% this year.

"As AI reshapes the threat landscape, we must continually evolve to protect our customers and enable them to adopt AI securely," CEO Nikesh Arora said in a release.

Palo Alto said annual recurring revenue for its next-generation security business jumped 66% from a year ago to $9.73 billion. Arora said the NGS ARR was one of the highest beats in the company's history.

The cybersecurity company bumped up guidance for fiscal year 2027 as businesses spend more on security in the age of AI.

Palo Alto expects adjusted earnings per share in the range of $4.26 to $4.30 and revenue in the range of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion. The forecasts topped the earnings of $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion in revenue expected by analysts.

Net income totaled $482 million, or 57 cents per share, up from $334 million, or 47 cents per share, a year ago.

Palo Alto Networks has been steadily acquiring companies to capitalize on demand for cyber tools in the age of AI.

Arora said the company's $4.5 billion all-stock deal for Applied Compute will help businesses secure open-weight models as adoption grows. The startup helps businesses run and customize their own AI models and marks a major investment for Palo Alto beyond cybersecurity.

"If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity," Arora said on an earnings call. "This could be bigger than what we do."

Outages from Microsoft, banks and air traffic control have heightened concerns around cyberattacks over the last week. U.S. officials have so far ruled out any malicious activity, but experts say the rapid acceleration in patching is straining dated systems.

As businesses discover more vulnerabilities, Arora said the company expects tens of thousands of virtual patches by the end of the fiscal year. 

"Whatever they do today is going to take three to six months, maybe nine months, depending on how complex and how tired their environment is," Arora said.

title: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’
excerpt: The Microsoft CEO downplayed the recent Outlook outage while noting that AI was causing both opportunities and new challenges for securing much of the connected world.
title_en: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’
excerpt_en: The Microsoft CEO downplayed the recent Outlook outage while noting that AI was causing both opportunities and new challenges for securing much of the connected world.
content_en:
During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.

“Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers \[a cooling device often used in data centers\] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”

In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.

Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”

“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.

“Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”

Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.

“We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact.

“The patch \[now\] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.”

title: Satya Nadella predicts AI agents will reshuffle the economics of the web

title_en: Satya Nadella predicts AI agents will reshuffle the economics of the web
excerpt_en: Microsoft's CEO says AI agents could disrupt advertising-driven business models, forcing companies like Amazon to rethink how they compete for customers.
content_en:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic.

Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago.

“The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” said Nadella. “And if you were monetizing ads because of the eyeballs, you now have to probably get down to essentially maybe CPC \[cost-per-click\] wins; maybe it’s more transactional,” he continued. “And so if you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will.”

The discussion turned to Amazon and its decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases on behalf of their users. Nadella suggested that companies trying to protect their existing business models could lose out to others that are more willing to embrace the AI agents. For instance, if Amazon continues blocking agents, another shopping platform such as Shopify, could allow them, and gain an advantage.

“I think this is going to be interesting,” he said, speaking to the changing models. “It’s the same thing that’s happening in other categories, right? Which is, if you’re in love with a particular business model, you have to kind of scramble,” he said.

title: Even His Own Officials Don’t Think Trump’s China Trip Will Lead to Progress on AI
excerpt: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal has made any negotiations around AI difficult, officials say.
title_en: Even His Own Officials Don’t Think Trump’s China Trip Will Lead to Progress on AI
excerpt_en: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal has made any negotiations around AI difficult, officials say.
content_en:
Ahead of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping on Thursday, administration officials privately tell *Inner Loop* they see little room for progress in alleviating AI safety and espionage concerns.

As he departed the White House, Trump left it an open question whether he would press Xi on Chinese interference in AI or the Nvidia scandal, as part of what officials say is an effort to not antagonize China during the summit.

But the fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, has made any negotiations around AI development fraught for the world's two largest economies, officials say.

Back in September, the Trump administration moved to set up an AI incident hotline between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese vice premier He Lifeng to account for situations just like this one. Unfortunately, the communication channel remains at the concept stage and is not operational.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters last week the US and Chinese governments had engaged in AI safety talks at a “technical level” since the hotline announcement, but admitted it was “still a work in progress.”

Trump officials have previously discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.

Part of the reason progress hasn’t been made yet is due to differing views on what the biggest risks are with AI—and both nations have different incentives on making incidents public, officials say.

In the US, Trump administration officials and tech leaders have been most worried about AI models becoming autonomous and misaligned, where they can operate beyond the bounds of human oversight.

But in China, government officials are widely understood to be more concerned about advanced open-weight models being used by critics and dissidents inside the country to undermine the Chinese Communist Party, officials say.

In an added complication, the Chinese government has appeared interested in using frontier AI models to gather intelligence domestically and abroad, and would be unlikely to report situations where their models went rogue, officials say.

Suspicions about mutual espionage have also exacerbated the distrust on any AI-related negotiations, officials tell *Inner Loop*. China has viewed the US as trying to stymie its AI development—and that was even before the Nvidia scandal.

China has forcefully bristled at allegations that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese intelligence agency, calling them “groundless” and a “smear.”

While Trump has sought to forge friendlier economic relations with China, the administration this week announced it would move forward with a new rule clamping down on China's ability to remotely access US-made AI chips in foreign data centers.

It marked a direct intervention by Trump in response to the alleged role of Megaspeed in the Nvidia scandal and criticism that a firm with ties to China had gained access to advanced AI chips. The rule could also prevent similar companies that might have their corporate parents in China from doing business with Nvidia, WIRED has previously reported.

*This is an edition of **Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter**. Read previous newsletters **here.***

title: Palmer Luckey warns AI-powered cyberattacks are outpacing defenses: ‘It’s time to start running’
excerpt: The Anduril co-founder says outdated technology is leaving systems vulnerable to a new wave of AI-enabled attacks.
title_en: Palmer Luckey warns AI-powered cyberattacks are outpacing defenses: ‘It’s time to start running’
excerpt_en: The Anduril co-founder says outdated technology is leaving systems vulnerable to a new wave of AI-enabled attacks.
content_en:
AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated technology systems can defend against them, Palmer Luckey warned at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Addressing the recent spate of tech outages, the Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder argued that older systems are struggling to keep pace with the new hacking capabilities enabled by AI and warned it was time to quicken the pace of securing our defenses.

“We’re seeing the natural effects of a lot of these advanced AI tools allowing for the creation of various exploits,” he said.

While government officials largely attributed the latest set of technical issues to companies rushing to patch their systems to protect against the new vulnerabilities AI has discovered, Luckey focused on the underlying security challenges facing organizations using outdated technology.

Luckey explained that U.S. adversaries are currently exploiting the mismatch between new attack capabilities and our defense capabilities. These attacks are being carried out for both strategic and financial reasons, and North Korea was particularly involved, he added.

The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, noted that U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance had canceled his appearance at the Times’ conference this week because of the recent tech outages, saying he now had to attend meetings about the matter.

Given the situation, Sorkin asked Luckey how worried we should be about all this.

“It depends on how well prepared you are,” was Luckey’s answer. (He then ominously warned, “You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough.”)

The tech executive argued that AI could ultimately give defenders the upper hand, but they’d have to move more quickly.

“In the long run, the advantages are going to accrue to the side that is most effectively using AI for defense,” Luckey said. “With the people who say that everything can be hacked — they are right, for now. That actually may be the case with certain new techniques that are coming along. But as of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers who are very fast-moving and using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” Luckey continued.

“And I think … people are going to have to pick up the pace,” he said. “It’s time to start running.”

title: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways
excerpt: The Trump administration announced plans to clamp down on China’s access to AI chips. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing.
title_en: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways
excerpt_en: The Trump administration announced plans to clamp down on China’s access to AI chips. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing.
content_en:
This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China. This is known as remote access.

But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place.

These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life.

As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling.

The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”)

It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips.

It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations.

The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead.

Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week.

The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China.

At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter.

According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.)

Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips.

But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue?

For one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies.

Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China.

Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished.

There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult.

This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment.

The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources.

I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life.

### Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of monday.com’s Elevate event

AI workflow automation is changing how businesses build applications and manage everyday work, raising questions about the role of established software platforms. As organizations experiment with AI-generated applications and autonomous agents, they must also determine how to maintain access controls, integrate existing systems and manage increasingly complex workflows.

The growing accessibility of AI development tools has prompted speculation that businesses could replace traditional software-as-a-service platforms with applications built for specific needs. But building an application and operating it securely across an enterprise present different challenges, according to Casey George, chief revenue officer of monday.com Ltd.

“We are seeing customers come back to a platform that’s integrated — that’s governed, that’s permissioned with their infrastructure, that is secure — like monday.com,” he told theCUBE. “I joke and say it was an expensive funeral, but we learned a lot. Customers learned a lot.”

George, along with executives and practitioners, spoke with host Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The discussions examined enterprise AI deployment, governance requirements and the challenges of scaling **AI workflow automation** across organizations. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Casey George:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of monday.com’s Elevate event:

### Insight #1: Deploying AI agents requires expertise and governance.

Making autonomous agents available to employees does not guarantee business returns. After an internal initiative produced more than 3,600 agents, monday.com established monday Frontier, an organization combining managed services and deployment engineers to help customers identify workflow bottlenecks and implement AI projects. The initiative addresses the implementation challenges involved in moving agents into productive use, according to Eran Zinman (pictured), co-founder and co-chief executive officer of monday.com.

“Adopting AI really requires expertise. I know how hard it is because we experienced ourselves that you have this amazing technology, but how do you actually use it?” he said during the event.

As organizations deploy AI agents, security teams must account for how access rights change across users, applications and environments. Incremental rollouts offer a way to test capabilities before expanding their reach, while permission management remains an ongoing responsibility, according to <u>Ryan Nigro</u>, security trust and enablement team lead at monday.com.

“It just comes to making sure that your users are properly being given just enough to do their roles but not too much to cause harm,” Nigro told theCUBE. “There’s no reason why a sales rep should have the ability to change your production environment.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Ryan Nigro:

### Insight #2: Shared dashboards improve operational visibility.

At Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., employees are using monday vibe, monday.com’s no-code application builder, to create custom tools. One executive dashboard replaces the manual process of copying charts into presentation slides while retaining the ability to export to PowerPoint, according to Kate Kenner, capability and community lead for strategic sourcing and planning at HPE.

“\[Executives\] knocked a whole bunch of the meetings off the calendar,” she told theCUBE. “Instead of weekly, now they’re monthly.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Kate Kenner:

At Lowe’s Cos. Inc., coordinating store setups and remodels once required tracking information across Microsoft Excel, emails and other communications. The retailer now uses monday.com to monitor individual store bays and dozens of simultaneous projects, according to Lanny Finley, director of remerch and new stores at Lowe’s.

“I can take the dashboard and see which projects are on track, which ones are at risk, and then make the appropriate actions and get the right partners in place to make the corrections to get everything back on track and completed,” he said during the event.

Lowe’s also developed an internal Green Dot Board to track issues such as missing components during store projects. The company is exploring additional automation that could initiate vendor orders when components are needed and close issues once replacements are installed, according to Brian Olms, senior business partner manager at Lowe’s, who joined Finley during the discussion.

“We needed a way to automate the process, make it more user-friendly \[and\] make it simpler. That’s what we started the Green Dot Board for,” he told theCUBE. “Here at Elevate, we’re seeing ways that we could even take it a step further and start to use agents and more automation and \[the\] vibe app.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Lanny Finley and Brian Olms:

### Insight #3: AI workflow automation expands organizational capacity.

For nonprofits facing growing demand, AI workflow automation offers a way to expand organizational capacity without placing additional administrative burdens on employees. At Feed the Children Inc., a two-person team oversees relationships with more than 500 community partners, according to Colleen Finn Ridenhour, chief growth and strategy officer at Feed the Children.

“Things from \[memorandums of understanding\] and legal contracts, annual renewals and compliance and reporting — it’s quite a lot. It’s been a very manual process, historically, for them to keep track of that all the time. We really want them focused on the human element of that job, which is bringing in new partners to help us scale our impact,” she told theCUBE.

The nonprofit uses monday.com’s forms, boards, automations and agents to coordinate partner activities and manage information. Employees can also build dashboards for specific needs, including budget tracking, while retaining human oversight of compliance-related work, according to Ridenhour.

“We’re not going to be able to scale our impact by just always asking people to work harder. \[We need to find\] ways to repeat a lot of these repetitive actions in a much easier way and \[share\] information so \[that\] people’s jobs get easier and it frees up their time to do the things that only they can do,” she said during the event.

title: More banks say customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked
excerpt: Citi is the latest major financial institution to put the breaks on personal finance AI agents.
title_en: More banks say customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked
excerpt_en: Citi is the latest major financial institution to put the breaks on personal finance AI agents.
content_en:
Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked.

AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.

But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.

“As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.”

JPMorgan and Bank of America, the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today.

Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch.

As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a new trust challenge.

Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”

Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability.

The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service, and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.

content_en:
### AI’s GPU focus meets a CPU reality check at Dell and AMD

Agentic AI is rewriting the business development playbook for chipmakers and server builders. Graphics processing units still grab the headlines, but as supercomputing and AI converge, the next wave of demand is landing on central processing units that must fit within data centers’ existing power budgets.

The shift has been building for years. Customers that hung more GPUs off a single CPU found they were starving expensive accelerators of data, leaving them idle, according to Scott Tease (pictured, left), vice president of business development for high-performance computing and sovereign AI at Advanced Micro Devices Inc.

“People have realized how important that CPU is in a GPU architecture. But beyond that, agentic is not necessarily just a GPU thing,” Tease said. “Agentic is going to be very CPU heavy because with agentic, what you’re looking at, you want to go very fast, but you also want concurrency.”

Tease and David Schmidt (right), vice president of PowerEdge product management at Dell Technologies Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the growing role of CPUs in agentic workloads and the challenges of balancing compute performance with data center power constraints. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Power limits reshape business development for compute

Dell and AMD have been building rack-scale AI platforms together, but power remains the binding constraint. When Dell began planning its portfolio 2.5 years ago, enterprise customers expected rack power requirements to remain at 15 to 20 kilowatts and said they often ran out of power before filling a rack, according to Schmidt. Dell responded with the PowerEdge R9825, a 3U server built on AMD’s sixth-generation EPYC 9006 processors.

“It’s been optimized for power efficiency and cooling efficiency,” Schmidt said. “That means we’re using less power to cool the system overall, and that’s power that we can return to our customers.”

That efficiency compounds at refresh time. A single EPYC 9006 server can take 13 legacy machines out of production while cutting the system power needed for cooling by 80 percent, Schmidt noted. Tease sees reclaimed power feeding agentic workloads, where agents could turn one researcher’s ideas into thousands of compute jobs.

“Same number of researchers, massive increase in the amount of compute. Agentic is going to continue to drive more and more IT, and we’ve got to find a way to power it,” Tease said.
